items.followUp: What does the word periodic mean in the context of the periodic table?

rubric.description: States that periodic means recurring at regular intervals.

rubric.why: Connects the meaning to the arrangement of elements.
rubric.description: States that element properties recur when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking recurrence to element properties.

modelAnswer: Periodic means recurring at regular intervals.
In the periodic table, the properties of elements repeat at regular intervals when elements are arranged by increasing atomic number.

items.followUp: Why is atomic number a more reliable basis for arranging elements than atomic mass?

rubric.description: States that atomic number is the number of protons in an atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying atomic number with proton number.

rubric.why: Explains why atomic number gives a suitable order.
rubric.description: States that atomic number determines the identity and periodic properties of an element, and/or that it keeps isotopes of an element together despite different masses.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid reason that atomic number gives the correct order.

modelAnswer: Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom and determines the identity of the element.
The properties of elements show periodicity with increasing atomic number; arranging by atomic number also keeps isotopes of an element together.

items.followUp: Why is bromine a liquid at room temperature while iodine is a solid?

rubric.why: Identifies the molecular form of iodine.
rubric.description: States that iodine exists as diatomic molecules in a solid molecular crystal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying molecular iodine.

rubric.why: Explains why iodine remains solid at room temperature.
rubric.description: States that attractions between iodine molecules are sufficiently strong, giving iodine a melting point above room temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining its solid state using intermolecular attraction or melting point.

modelAnswer: Iodine exists as diatomic I₂ molecules arranged in a molecular crystal.
The attractions between its molecules are strong enough to give iodine a melting point above room temperature, so it is solid.

items.followUp: Name three elements that are liquid at, or close to, ordinary room temperature.

rubric.why: Recognizes the two elements that are liquid at ordinary room temperature.
rubric.description: Names mercury and bromine, the elements that are liquids at ordinary room temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both mercury and bromine.

rubric.why: Recognizes an element that becomes liquid close to room temperature.
rubric.description: Names a third element with a melting point close to room temperature, such as gallium or cesium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid third element; gallium and cesium become liquid when slightly warmed above ordinary room temperature.

modelAnswer: Mercury (Hg) and bromine (Br₂) are liquid at ordinary room temperature.
Gallium (Ga) is also a near-room-temperature liquid; it melts when warmed slightly above room temperature.

items.followUp: Write any three properties of noble gases.

rubric.why: Gives a characteristic physical form of noble gases.
rubric.description: States that noble gases exist as single atoms (are monoatomic).

rubric.why: Gives the characteristic low reactivity of noble gases.
rubric.description: States that noble gases are chemically inert or very unreactive.

modelAnswer: Noble gases are monoatomic; they exist as single atoms.
They are colourless and odourless gases.
They are chemically inert because their outer electron shells are complete.

items.followUp: How can environmental education help people protect the environment?

rubric.why: States an immediate objective of environmental education.
rubric.description: States that it develops awareness and understanding of the environment and its problems.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for awareness or understanding of environmental issues.

rubric.why: States the practical outcome of environmental education.
rubric.description: States that it encourages people to take part in solving environmental problems or protecting the environment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an action-oriented objective.

modelAnswer: The main objective of environmental education is to create awareness and understanding of the environment and its problems.
It encourages people to participate in solving these problems and protecting the environment.

items.followUp: Explain how carbon monoxide interferes with oxygen transport in the body.

rubric.why: Identifies the blood component affected by carbon monoxide.
rubric.description: States that carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in the blood.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying haemoglobin as the target.

rubric.why: Explains the harmful effect on the body.
rubric.description: States that this reduces oxygen transport and may cause suffocation, unconsciousness, or death.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the reduced oxygen supply or a serious consequence.

modelAnswer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in the blood to form carboxyhaemoglobin.
This reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen and can cause suffocation, unconsciousness, or death.

items.followUp: Give one difference between an organic compound and an inorganic compound, with an example of each.

rubric.why: Gives the typical composition of organic compounds.
rubric.description: States that organic compounds generally contain carbon bonded to hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the carbon–hydrogen distinction.

rubric.why: Contrasts inorganic compounds with organic compounds.
rubric.description: States that inorganic compounds are generally mineral compounds and usually lack carbon–hydrogen bonds; a suitable example may also be given.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid contrast or example. Note that some carbon-containing substances, such as carbon dioxide and carbonates, are inorganic.

modelAnswer: Organic compounds generally contain carbon bonded to hydrogen, for example methane (CH₄).
Inorganic compounds are generally mineral compounds and usually do not contain carbon–hydrogen bonds, for example sodium chloride (NaCl).
